CleanSpark Climbs 5% as Bitcoin Miners Outrun the Coin; Strategy Rises 4%
Bitcoin mining stocks are surging at a rate that dwarfs the coin itself, and the gap between equity gains and spot price raises a question the tape alone cannot answer.
Published September 17, 2026, 9:34am ET · 4 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.

TheBitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining complex is repricing faster than the coin itself Thursday morning, and CleanSpark sits near the front of that move. Those sector gains are running at multiples of Bitcoin’s own advance, which points to a sector-wide re-rating rather than a coin-driven bid.
The CoinShares Bitcoin Mining and Digital Power ETF (NASDAQ:WGMI) is up 6% to $47.20, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 1% to $763.81. Bitcoin is up 1.39% to $76,633.43 over the trailing 24 hours.
CleanSpark (NASDAQ:CLSK | CLSK Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $13.49 in Thursday morning trading, keeping CleanSpark near the front of a broader mining rally with no fresh company disclosure behind the move. Meanwhile, Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shares are up 4% to $130.71, a smaller gain than the pure miners but still a multiple of the coin’s own advance.
The gap between the equity gains and Bitcoin’s own move is the story here. Bitcoin’s 1.39% advance doesn’t account for CleanSpark’s 5% jump, and the CoinShares fund’s matching 6% gain confirms that this is a group bid rather than a CleanSpark-specific reaction.
With no CleanSpark press release, filing or transcript landing this morning, the plain mechanism looks like a sector-wide re-rating of high-beta crypto equities. A short squeeze can’t be ruled out as a contributor, though no fresh short interest data verifies that read, and it stays a possible rather than a confirmed driver of CleanSpark’s tape.
CleanSpark’s 5% advance is running against a Bitcoin quote that has already given back ground from earlier month highs, so the equity bid isn’t simply a reflection of a strong coin session. That divergence is the pattern that keeps drawing attention to miner names when the group catches a bid, and CleanSpark’s move fits the profile.
The U.S. Senate cloture vote on the Clarity Act failed on September 15, when the measure fell short of the sixty votes it needed to advance. That defeat is two sessions old and crypto-linked equities rebounded the following session, which places it in the background of today’s move rather than the trigger for it.
Strategy, the corporate Bitcoin proxy in this group, tends to trade as leveraged exposure to the coin. Strategy’s 4% gain sitting below the pure miners’ moves is consistent with a bid concentrated in operating mining equities rather than treasury vehicles, and it reinforces the read that the sector, not the coin, is doing the work today.
CleanSpark’s bull case rests on the size of the gap between the equity moves and Bitcoin’s advance. A mining complex repricing faster than the coin suggests the market is paying for something beyond spot exposure, and CleanSpark’s version of that something is its data center build-out and the prospect of leasing capacity to artificial intelligence tenants.
The complication is that a move this size with no accompanying disclosure can unwind as fast as it arrived. CleanSpark’s gain matches the CoinShares fund almost exactly, which says the bid isn’t CleanSpark-specific and can reverse if the sector bid fades before the close.
The company’s operating profile leans on scaling its mining fleet while carving out space for adjacent digital infrastructure, and any signal that a large tenant sits behind the current data center footprint would change the story materially (we profiled seven suppliers riding the AI data-center buildout, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here). Absent such a signal today, CleanSpark’s move reads as market appetite for the theme rather than confirmation of the theme.
The bear case for CleanSpark is straightforward. Sector re-ratings without accompanying company news tend to fade, and CleanSpark’s high beta cuts both ways: a subsequent leg lower in Bitcoin, or simply an unwind of today’s sector bid, can pull CleanSpark stock back through $13 as quickly as it advanced above.
Investors can watch for whether CleanSpark stock holds at $13.40 through the afternoon. A hold at these levels keeps the technical picture constructive; a give-back into the red would confirm the morning move was a sector reflex rather than a durable re-rating for CleanSpark.
Traders may want to keep an eye on whether the CoinShares fund and CleanSpark stock stay coupled for the rest of the session, since a decoupling would flag a company-specific bid or seller worth investigating. Shareholders should size their positions to account for CLSK stock’s high beta and the risk that a single-day rally without company disclosure often mean-reverts inside a few sessions.

CleanSpark Closes $2.276 Billion Senior Secured Notes Offering To Fund Sandersville Data Center Development
CleanSpark has completed its $2.276 billion senior secured notes offering, securing substantial debt financing to support the development of its data center in Sandersville, Georgia.
The notes were issued by CSDC Finance I, LLC, a wholly owned indirect subsidiary of CleanSpark, and carry an annual interest rate of 7.875%. The offering closed on September 25, 2026, with the notes scheduled to mature in October 2031.
The financing represents a major capital commitment to CleanSpark’s data center infrastructure business as the company develops large-scale computing facilities.
The notes were sold in a private offering to qualified institutional buyers and certain investors outside the United States.
They were issued at 98.5% of their $2.276 billion aggregate principal amount, meaning the cash received before expenses is lower than the notes’ face value.
CleanSpark intends to use the net proceeds to finance the remaining construction costs associated with its Sandersville data center, reimburse certain prior equity contributions related to the facility, and establish debt service reserves.
The financing was originally announced on September 18, when CleanSpark disclosed the pricing and expected closing date.
Completion of the offering establishes a dedicated source of long-term capital for the Sandersville project.
The financing has been structured at the subsidiary level, with CSDC Finance serving as the issuer.
The notes are fully and unconditionally guaranteed by CSRE Properties Sandersville, LLC, another CleanSpark subsidiary.
They are secured by first-priority liens on substantially all assets of the issuer and subsidiary guarantor, subject to specified exclusions.
The collateral package also includes the ownership interests in CSDC Finance held by its direct parent, CSDC Holdings I, LLC.
These arrangements establish the asset security supporting the debt and distinguish the offering from an unsecured corporate financing.
CleanSpark has also agreed to provide a completion guarantee for the Sandersville facility.
Under that arrangement, the parent company will provide additional funding if the bond proceeds and other available funds are insufficient to complete construction within the required timetable.
The guarantee provides an additional layer of support for the project during its development.
The notes will bear interest at 7.875% annually, with payments scheduled twice a year on April 1 and October 1.
The first interest payment is scheduled for April 1, 2027, and the notes will mature on October 1, 2031, unless redeemed or repurchased earlier under their terms.
The financing also includes provisions for scheduled principal amortization tied to the project’s debt service coverage requirements.
Following the project’s final commencement date, principal will be repaid semiannually in amounts designed to achieve the target project debt service coverage ratio specified in the bond documents.
The agreement contains customary covenants and events of default.
Certain changes in ownership may require the issuer to offer to repurchase the notes at 101% of their outstanding principal amount, plus accrued and unpaid interest.
The financing supports CleanSpark’s strategy of developing data center infrastructure capable of serving increasingly demanding computing applications.
CleanSpark reports controlling more than 1.8 gigawatts of power, land, and data center assets across the United States.
Its business combines experience in Bitcoin mining, energy infrastructure, and large-scale computing operations.
The company is pursuing opportunities to expand its data center platform as demand for computing capacity increases.
The Sandersville financing provides capital dedicated to completing a major facility within that infrastructure portfolio.
The transaction also establishes a financing structure under which the project’s assets and future cash flows support long-term debt obligations.
With the offering completed, CleanSpark will continue developing the Sandersville facility while managing the construction, financial, and operating commitments established under the notes.

Should You Buy CleanSpark (CLSK) Stock Before Its AI Pivot Pays Off?
As digital infrastructure assets undergo a monumental shift and bitcoin miners are becoming AI landlords, CleanSpark Inc. (NASDAQ:CLSK) is attempting to pivot from a pure-play, volatile cryptocurrency miner into a contracted, high-performance compute host. While historical multi-year revenue growth and operational cash flow generation have remained tied to unpredictable crypto cycles, CleanSpark's evolving balance sheet health, long-term return on invested capital/ROIC, and free cash flow conversion profile now hinge on converting power-heavy infrastructure into predictable, long-duration lease streams.
Should You Buy CleanSpark (CLSK) Stock Before Its AI Pivot Pays Off?
That capital-intensive evolution reached a key milestone on September 18, when CleanSpark priced $2.276 billion in 7.875% senior secured notes due 2031 at 98.5% of face value to institutional buyers. This massive debt raise directly supports the company's fundamental transition: the proceeds are earmarked to complete construction at its Sandersville Facility, reimburse equity previously deployed into the site, and fund debt service reserves. Backed by first-priority liens on Sandersville assets and a CleanSpark completion guarantee, this financing provides the liquidity required to convert heavy capital expenditure into durable, recurring cash flows.
The strategic thesis behind Sandersville looks considerably more grounded than a standard mining facility expansion. On August 6, when CleanSpark released results for the quarter ended June 30, management disclosed a landmark 20-year, $6.6 billion triple-net lease at Sandersville with a high investment-grade tenant.
This contract secures two decades of contracted, non-mining revenue, insulating the facility from daily bitcoin price volatility. Furthermore, the equity portion for Sandersville is fully funded, and CleanSpark has already pre-paid and ordered long-lead equipment to ensure it hits its ready-for-service target date. Pre-ordering critical equipment hedges against supply chain delays that plague high-density data center buildouts, reinforcing management's drive to transform power capacity into stable, long-term cash flow compounding.
However, executing this infrastructure pivot carries substantial near-term balance sheet friction and margin pressure. For the fiscal quarter ended June 30, CleanSpark reported a challenging set of financial metrics: top-line revenue dropped 30.5% year-over-year to $138.0 million, down from $198.6 million in the prior-year period. Operating profitability and margins suffered heavily, swinging from net income of $257.4 million to a net loss of $239.8 million ($0.89 per basic share). Adjusted EBITDA experienced a sharp reversal, plunging to negative $113.0 million compared to positive $377.7 million a year earlier.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.
In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

There is also a key difference between the ABR and Zacks Rank when it comes to freshness. When you look at the ABR, it may not be up-to-date. CleanSpark seeks $2.227 billion in secured notes for Meta-backed Sandersville campus
Bitcoin miner turned AI factory CleanSpark (NASDAQ: CLSK) plans to offer $2.227 billion of senior secured notes due 2031, according to a company filing Thursday. The filing did not disclose the proposed coupon rate.
CleanSpark intends to use the proceeds to complete its Sandersville, Georgia, data center, reimburse prior equity contributions and fund debt-service reserves. The private offering targets qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A and non-U.S. investors under Regulation S.
The 175 MW critical IT campus is leased for 20 years to Anviran, a wholly owned Meta subsidiary. Meta guarantees rent and operating expenses under the lease, which carries a 3% annual escalator and about $6.6 billion of contracted payments over its base term.

The notes will be guaranteed by CSRE Properties Sandersville, another subsidiary of the issuer. First-priority liens will cover substantially all assets of the issuer and CSRE Properties, subject to exclusions, as well as the equity interests in CSDC Finance I held by its direct parent.
CleanSpark will also provide a completion guarantee. That obligation requires the parent to fund the issuer as needed to finish Sandersville on time if proceeds from the notes prove insufficient, leaving CleanSpark exposed to construction funding risk through completion.
CleanSpark's investor presentation estimates development costs at about $11.9 million per IT MW and average annual net operating income of roughly $330 million. The company models an approximately 100% triple-net lease structure, with rent beginning November 30, 2027, after completion of the first network hall.
"We continue making strong construction progress at our Sandersville site as we execute for our high-investment grade tenant," CleanSpark CEO and Chairman Matt Schultz said in the company's August operating update.
Debt amortization is modeled to begin when construction finishes, which CleanSpark expects in March 2028. The illustrative schedule uses a 1.275x debt-service coverage ratio, while lease support coverage starts at 2.9x in 2028 and declines to 2.6x before rising as principal amortizes.
Sandersville is the first signed AI data center lease within CleanSpark's 1.8 GW contracted power portfolio. The same tenant, Meta, has an exclusivity arrangement covering CleanSpark's Texas sites, where 885 MW received conditional ERCOT classifications, but that arrangement is not a binding lease.

TheBitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) mining complex is repricing faster than the coin itself Thursday morning, and CleanSpark sits near the front of that move. Those sector gains are running at multiples of Bitcoin’s own advance, which points to a sector-wide re-rating rather than a coin-driven bid.
The CoinShares Bitcoin Mining and Digital Power ETF (NASDAQ:WGMI) is up 6% to $47.20, while the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 1% to $763.81. Bitcoin is up 1.39% to $76,633.43 over the trailing 24 hours.
CleanSpark (NASDAQ:CLSK | CLSK Price Prediction) stock is up 5% to $13.49 in Thursday morning trading, keeping CleanSpark near the front of a broader mining rally with no fresh company disclosure behind the move. Meanwhile, Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) shares are up 4% to $130.71, a smaller gain than the pure miners but still a multiple of the coin’s own advance.
The gap between the equity gains and Bitcoin’s own move is the story here. Bitcoin’s 1.39% advance doesn’t account for CleanSpark’s 5% jump, and the CoinShares fund’s matching 6% gain confirms that this is a group bid rather than a CleanSpark-specific reaction.
With no CleanSpark press release, filing or transcript landing this morning, the plain mechanism looks like a sector-wide re-rating of high-beta crypto equities. A short squeeze can’t be ruled out as a contributor, though no fresh short interest data verifies that read, and it stays a possible rather than a confirmed driver of CleanSpark’s tape.
CleanSpark’s 5% advance is running against a Bitcoin quote that has already given back ground from earlier month highs, so the equity bid isn’t simply a reflection of a strong coin session. That divergence is the pattern that keeps drawing attention to miner names when the group catches a bid, and CleanSpark’s move fits the profile.
The U.S. Senate cloture vote on the Clarity Act failed on September 15, when the measure fell short of the sixty votes it needed to advance. That defeat is two sessions old and crypto-linked equities rebounded the following session, which places it in the background of today’s move rather than the trigger for it.
Strategy, the corporate Bitcoin proxy in this group, tends to trade as leveraged exposure to the coin. Strategy’s 4% gain sitting below the pure miners’ moves is consistent with a bid concentrated in operating mining equities rather than treasury vehicles, and it reinforces the read that the sector, not the coin, is doing the work today.
CleanSpark’s bull case rests on the size of the gap between the equity moves and Bitcoin’s advance. A mining complex repricing faster than the coin suggests the market is paying for something beyond spot exposure, and CleanSpark’s version of that something is its data center build-out and the prospect of leasing capacity to artificial intelligence tenants.
The complication is that a move this size with no accompanying disclosure can unwind as fast as it arrived. CleanSpark’s gain matches the CoinShares fund almost exactly, which says the bid isn’t CleanSpark-specific and can reverse if the sector bid fades before the close.
The company’s operating profile leans on scaling its mining fleet while carving out space for adjacent digital infrastructure, and any signal that a large tenant sits behind the current data center footprint would change the story materially (we profiled seven suppliers riding the AI data-center buildout, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here). Absent such a signal today, CleanSpark’s move reads as market appetite for the theme rather than confirmation of the theme.
The bear case for CleanSpark is straightforward. Sector re-ratings without accompanying company news tend to fade, and CleanSpark’s high beta cuts both ways: a subsequent leg lower in Bitcoin, or simply an unwind of today’s sector bid, can pull CleanSpark stock back through $13 as quickly as it advanced above.
Investors can watch for whether CleanSpark stock holds at $13.40 through the afternoon. A hold at these levels keeps the technical picture constructive; a give-back into the red would confirm the morning move was a sector reflex rather than a durable re-rating for CleanSpark.
Traders may want to keep an eye on whether the CoinShares fund and CleanSpark stock stay coupled for the rest of the session, since a decoupling would flag a company-specific bid or seller worth investigating. Shareholders should size their positions to account for CLSK stock’s high beta and the risk that a single-day rally without company disclosure often mean-reverts inside a few sessions.

CleanSpark has completed one of the largest financing transactions of the year for a publicly traded Bitcoin miner, closing $2.276 billion of senior secured notes.
The company announced the completed transaction late on September 25, moving the financing from a capital-markets proposal into cash that can now be deployed across the business.
CleanSpark Is Funding More Than Bitcoin Miners
CleanSpark says the proceeds will be used in part to expand its data-center infrastructure and refinance existing debt.
That distinction matters as the economics of the mining sector continue to change.
Bitcoin miners still earn revenue by operating ASIC hardware and selling or holding the BTC they produce.

CleanSpark has been building around that overlap.

The size of the deal is notable.
Mining is a capital-intensive business, and borrowing more than $2 billion introduces a significant fixed obligation onto the balance sheet.
That can work well when operating cash flow is strong and infrastructure investment generates attractive returns.
It becomes more uncomfortable when Bitcoin prices fall, mining difficulty rises or power economics deteriorate.
That tension has always existed in the sector.
Mining companies need to spend heavily to stay competitive, but taking on too much capital-market risk can turn a downturn into a balance-sheet problem.
CleanSpark appears willing to make the trade.
The company has spent the past several years increasing scale, upgrading its fleet and accumulating infrastructure in the United States.

LAS VEGAS September 18, 2026 — CleanSpark, Inc. (Nasdaq: CLSK) (“CleanSpark” or the “Company”), a market-leading data center developer, today announced that its wholly owned subsidiary, CSDC Finance I, LLC (the “Issuer”), has priced a $2.276 billion offering of 7.875% senior secured notes due 2031 (the “Notes”) at a price equal to 98.500% of their principal amount. The Notes will be sold in a private offering to persons reasonably believed to be qualified institutional buyers in reliance on Rule 144A under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”) and to non-U.S. persons outside of the United States pursuant to Regulation S under the Securities Act. The offering is expected to close on September 25, 2026, subject to customary closing conditions.
The Issuer intends to use the net proceeds from the offering (a) to finance the remaining cost of the build out of the data center (the “Sandersville Facility”), (b) to reimburse the Company for certain prior equity contributions made in respect of the Sandersville Facility, and (c) to fund debt service reserves.
The Notes will be fully and unconditionally guaranteed by CSRE Properties Sandersville, LLC, a wholly owned direct subsidiary of the Issuer (“CSRE Properties”). The Notes and related note guarantee will be secured by first-priority liens on (i) substantially all assets of the Issuer and CSRE Properties, other than certain excluded property, and (ii) all equity interests of the Issuer held by CSDC Holdings I, LLC, a Delaware limited liability company and the direct parent company of the Issuer.
CleanSpark will provide a customary completion guarantee with respect to the Sandersville Facility, under which it will fund the Issuer as necessary to ensure the timely completion of the Sandersville Facility in the event that the proceeds of the Notes are insufficient to do so.
The offering is subject to market and other conditions, and there can be no assurance as to whether, when or on what terms the offering may be completed.
The Notes have not been registered under the Securities Act or securities laws of any other jurisdiction, and the Notes may not be offered or sold in the United States absent registration or an applicable exemption from registration under the Securities Act and any applicable state securities laws.
